title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
gist: An Origina-commissioned survey of 2,018 CIOs at 10,000+ employee firms found enterprises spend on average 28 percent of software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations and licensing changes; 95 percent paid for a vendor-driven change they believed would hurt. Origina sells independent software maintenance, so the report carries potential bias.

insights.claim: Enterprises spend on average 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations and licensing changes, according to a survey of 2,018 CIOs and senior IT decision-makers at companies with 10,000+ employees.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Forced-upgrade spend is a large, recurring revenue stream for incumbent enterprise software vendors.

insights.claim: Ninety-five percent of respondents said their organization paid for a vendor-driven upgrade, migration or licensing change in the past three years that it believed would reduce performance, reliability or business value, and 53 percent did so more than once.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Customers feel coerced, which makes incumbent revenue exposed if credible alternatives or regulation appear.

insights.claim: Seventy-six percent of respondents say their organization has very little real leverage in negotiations and 80 percent say moving away from major vendors would cause significant disruption.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: High switching costs underpin vendor pricing power.

insights.claim: The survey's reported cost of forced upgrades falls on innovation (36 percent), human resources (32 percent), security (31 percent) and customer-facing investment (31 percent).
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Locked-in software spend crowds out other IT investment categories.

insights.claim: Every survey respondent runs at least one of IBM, HCL, VMware/Broadcom or SAP at meaningful scale, though the report names no vendor as forcing upgrades.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The sample is concentrated among large-vendor customers, so results indicate exposure of these vendors' installed bases.

insights.claim: The survey's sponsor Origina provides maintenance for enterprise software and promotes independent software maintenance as a way to regain control of budgets, indicating potential bias.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.locator: Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance

insights.claim: Ninety-one percent of respondents would support laws giving enterprises protections comparable to long-term residential tenants, with 1 percent opposed.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Signals latent demand for regulation of enterprise software licensing.

insights.claim: Report co-author Marshall Van Alstyne advises CIOs to negotiate the exit before the entry, setting migration assistance pricing and caps on renewal and expansion prices in initial contracts.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Contract terms on exit and renewal caps are the practical mitigation for buyers.
insights.quote: negotiate the exit before the entry

insights.claim: Origina CEO Tomás O'Leary argues that saying yes to unwanted upgrades is often rational when the alternative is losing support on business-critical systems.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Support-termination threats are the lever vendors use to force upgrades.
insights.quote: When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response

insights.claim: Liberty Mutual CIO James McGlennon said an upgrade cycle can occupy top technical workers for the better part of a year, a recurring drag on capacity.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Upgrade cycles carry hidden labor cost beyond license fees.
insights.locator: In a statement accompanying the survey
